libSQL is a SQLite fork, so JOIN and ORDER BY are core SQL. FR-IDX-02's tag filter is an ordinary junction table, FR-IDX-01 orders by publication date, FR-HOME-03 groups by year - all single queries with no application-side assembly.
Full PostgreSQL is a strict superset of what FR-IDX-01, FR-IDX-02 and FR-HOME-03 require. No capability gap of any kind at this corpus size.

Document model. FR-IDX-02's tag filter needs either tags embedded per essay or an aggregation lookup, and FR-IDX-03 separately requires enumerating the distinct tag set in use - which embedding makes expensive and duplicative. Both other options get this from one junction table.

The client communicates over HTTP rather than holding a long-lived TCP session, so there is no connection pool for short-lived serverless invocations to exhaust. This is the property AD-5 and ADR 0002's execution model make decisive.

Workable, but the vendor ships a purpose-built serverless driver precisely because pooled Postgres connections are a problem in this setting - the existence of that driver is the evidence of the hazard. VERIFY whether the pooled endpoint is included on the free plan.

Connection limits are per-cluster while serverless functions open connections per invocation, so the free tier's limit becomes a ceiling on concurrent requests rather than on data. VERIFY the M0 connection limit.

SQLite provides FTS5, so FR-IDX-05 needs no separate search service. VERIFY whether the hosted platform exposes FTS5 on the free plan; if not, FR-IDX-05 falls back to LIKE, which is adequate at fifty essays but is a limit being accepted rather than measured.
PostgreSQL full-text search via tsvector is built in with no extension to enable, and supports the title-over-body ranking FR-IDX-05's relevance clause would want if it were retained.
Text indexes exist and would satisfy FR-IDX-05, but they are a different query model to learn alongside the document model itself, against C4's cap.

A libSQL database is a local file with no server process to install or run. This is what makes NFR-REL-02's restore drill cheap - the drill requires dropping every table and rebuilding repeatedly, which is a file deletion rather than a reprovisioning.

Requires either a local PostgreSQL installation on both the desktop and the laptop (Charter section 3 lists two machines) or a second cloud branch. Branching is the better route; VERIFY branch count on the free plan.
Requires a local server installation on both machines or a second cluster. Same shape of cost as Neon, with the added novelty of the document model during the NFR-REL-02 drill.

PROVISIONAL pending VERIFY. This is mine to answer, not a vendor's. Count only what I have shipped with - built, deployed, and debugged - per the Chapter 5 definition, then set all three scores in this criterion from that.
PROVISIONAL pending VERIFY. Same basis. Note that SQL knowledge transfers between Turso and Neon, so if either is familiar the other is partly familiar too - which is not true of the third option.

PROVISIONAL pending VERIFY. Charter section 3 names MongoDB as one of two learn-slots for the semester, so it was a planned novelty rather than an accidental one. That is a reason it belongs in this matrix, not a reason to score it higher.

On-demand invalidation of an already-rendered route is first-party on this platform rather than supplied by an adapter, so there is no intermediate layer that can lag the framework. FR-SYS-02's sixty-second ceiling depends entirely on this mechanism. VERIFY the current API name and its free-plan availability.

Incremental regeneration for this framework arrives through an adapter rather than natively. VERIFY the current support level and any free-plan restriction - this single cell decides the whole decision, which currently sits at the coin-flip threshold.
Static file hosting only. Content changes require a rebuild and redeploy, so FR-SYS-02 is unreachable by any configuration. Scored zero rather than low because this is disqualifying, not weak.
Serverless functions run the FR-CONT-01 write path and the FR-AUTH-01 middleware check in the request path, which is what the admin side requires to exist at all.
Equivalent function runtime. No difference from Vercel on this criterion.
No server runtime. FR-AUTH-02 cannot compare a passphrase against an environment variable and FR-CONT-01 cannot insert a row. Disqualifying, so zero.

The platform's own Git integration deploys on push to main, which means no deploy credential exists to store or leak - it removes a secret from NFR-SEC-02's surface rather than protecting one.
Equivalent Git integration with the same benefit.
Native to the repository host, so deployment is the simplest of the three. Again irrelevant given the disqualifying scores above.

Dependency D1 already names Netlify and Render as the documented fallback, and NFR-PORT-01's browser testing is host-agnostic. Scored 4 rather than 5 because the fallback is written down but has not been exercised.
Symmetrical - Vercel or Render would be the fallback. Same unexercised status.
Nothing to migrate to that is more constrained, and migrating away would mean adopting one of the other two anyway - so the option offers no portability benefit it does not already concede.

Matches the requirement exactly. A1 and C6 establish exactly one privileged user who may do everything, which reduces authorisation to a yes-or-no on knowing one secret. No user table exists anywhere in the data inventory.

Built around identity providers and persisted user records. A credentials-only configuration is possible but works against the library's grain, and brings session-store and adapter concepts that exist to solve a problem C6 rules out.
A managed user directory is the product being purchased, and C6 says there are no users to manage. Scored 2 rather than 0 because it would technically satisfy FR-AUTH-01 through 03.

One small signing dependency and one middleware file. C4's two learn-slots are already spent by ADR 0001 and ADR 0004, so anything larger is a third new thing. VERIFY the signing library's current version and licence.
A distinct framework to learn, with its own configuration model, against a 60-75 hour budget and a scope-cut trigger already dated to 8 November.
A new external service plus its SDK, and a new entry on the free-tier watch list that can begin billing.
No third party sits in the authentication path, so there is nothing to bill and nothing to add to the watch list.
An open-source library with no hosted component, so the same applies.
PROVISIONAL pending VERIFY. Read the vendor pricing page for the free-plan monthly-active-user allowance and, more importantly under C3, whether exceeding it bills or blocks.

Roughly forty lines: one login route, one cookie, one middleware matcher. Scored 4 rather than 5 because FR-AUTH-04's redirect validation and the environment-conditional Secure flag are both easy to get wrong on a first attempt.
Less code to write but a configuration model to learn first, and the credentials path is the least-documented route through it.
Fast once configured, but adds account setup, application registration, and callback URL configuration across two environments.

Deliberately the lowest score of the three on this criterion. Signing, cookie flags and redirect validation are all my code, which is why NFR-SEC-02 and NFR-SEC-03 exist in the specification at all. The cost of this option is paid in verification effort rather than avoided.
The signing and session handling are library code reviewed by many people rather than mine.
The credential never touches my code and the provider carries the breach risk. This is the one criterion where the rejected options are genuinely better.

Pre-renders routes and exposes a first-party call to invalidate one after a write - the only mechanism on the table that satisfies FR-SYS-02's sixty seconds and NFR-PERF-01's 2.5 s LCP at the same time. VERIFY the current API name and signature.

Content-focused static generation is its strength; on-demand invalidation of an already-built page is its weaker story. VERIFY the current capability before treating this score as settled, since it is the only criterion separating Astro from the winner.

Client-rendered pages fetch essay text after load, so FR-SYS-02 becomes trivial and NFR-PERF-01 is lost - every reader waits on a database round trip before any text appears. Scored 1 rather than 0 because caching could partly recover it, at the cost of rebuilding what the other options give free.
FR-CONT-01's write path and FR-AUTH-01's middleware live in the same application as the public pages, so one deployment and one environment-variable set cover both.
Server endpoints exist and would carry the admin write path, but the split between static and server rendering is a mode to configure per route rather than a default.
Two deployables, two environment-variable sets, and a CORS boundary between them. Against C1's hours this is the dominant cost of the option.

Charter section 3 lists React as already known. The component model transfers directly, so the novelty is the server execution model rather than an entire framework - which is what keeps the declared novelty load inside C4's cap.
Its own component model, with React embeddable inside it. Partial transfer of existing knowledge, plus a second model to hold in mind.
Plain React with no framework conventions layered over it, so existing knowledge transfers completely. This is the one criterion the option wins.

The remark and rehype pipeline handles FR-READ-02's formatting and FR-READ-03's footnotes as plugins rather than code I write. VERIFY the footnote plugin's package name, current version, and which syntax dialect it parses - a dialect mismatch renders markers as literal text with no error.

A first-class content pipeline with frontmatter is closer to the shape of an essay corpus than anything the other options offer by default. Astro wins this criterion outright and it is a real loss in not taking it.
The same remark and rehype libraries are available, but rendering markdown in the browser adds it to the client bundle, working against NFR-PERF-03's 150 KB JavaScript ceiling.
One repository, one build, one host, one CI pipeline, one environment-variable set. This is what C1's hours and C2's resumable-work requirement can actually carry.
Equivalent - one deployable covering both static pages and server endpoints.
Two services to deploy, version, and keep in step, plus a second thing to break during weeks 9-12 when C1 has no slack for it.
